title: USCIS Now Checks Green Card Sponsors' Credit History Under Revised Form I-864
excerpt: A new privacy release in the updated Affidavit of Support lets immigration officers pull sponsors' credit reports directly from consumer reporting agencies.
body:
• USCIS began accepting a revised Form I-864 on August 31, 2026, which includes a privacy release authorizing the agency to pull sponsors' credit reports directly from consumer reporting agencies.
  • No minimum credit score has been specified, and immigration attorneys say it remains unclear how USCIS will use the credit data in evaluating sponsorship eligibility.
  • Sponsors with a credit or security freeze should lift it immediately to avoid processing delays, according to the American Immigration Lawyers' Association.
  • The change coincides with a broader public charge rule taking effect September 18 that gives officers wider discretion to weigh sponsors' financial histories.

Green card sponsors in the United States now face direct credit scrutiny from immigration authorities under a revised version of Form I-864, the Affidavit of Support required for most family-based and some employment-based immigration petitions. USCIS began accepting the updated form on August 31, 2026, with no grace period for the previous edition.

The most consequential change is a new privacy release embedded in the form. By signing, sponsors authorize USCIS to request their credit-related information directly from one or more consumer reporting agencies — a power the agency previously did not have in the I-864 process.

What the Credit Check Means

USCIS has not published a minimum credit score threshold or spelled out exactly what financial factors would lead to a rejection. Neither a missed credit card payment nor a past bankruptcy has been formally identified as a disqualifier, according to immigration experts.

What is clear is that officers will have access to a sponsor's full credit profile—payment history, outstanding debts, liens, and bankruptcy filings—and can use that information to assess whether the sponsor is genuinely able to support the immigrant they are sponsoring.

"If sponsors have a credit or security freeze on their consumer or credit reports, USCIS may not be able to access the financial information that they need to evaluate a sponsor's eligibility."

— American Immigration Lawyers' Association (AILA)

The American Immigration Lawyers' Association has advised sponsors who maintain a credit freeze — a common identity-theft protection measure — to lift it before filing. A freeze does not erase credit history, but it could block USCIS from accessing the reports it now considers part of the evaluation, potentially causing delays or outright rejections.

Income Requirements Unchanged — But the Bar Is Higher

The revised form does not change the baseline income requirement. Sponsors must still demonstrate household income at or above 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines. However, immigration attorneys say the credit review effectively raises the bar by giving adjudicators a far more detailed view of a sponsor's financial reliability than income documentation alone.

This matters in the context of a separate but related policy shift. On September 18, 2026, a new public charge rule takes effect that grants USCIS officers significantly broader discretion in evaluating whether an immigrant is likely to become a public charge. Under the new framework, officers can weigh nearly any means-tested public benefit tied to low income—including Medicaid, SNAP, and housing assistance—when adjudicating green card applications filed on or after that date.

A Tighter Sponsorship Landscape

The two changes together reshape the sponsorship landscape. The affidavit of support, once considered a near-automatic safeguard in family-based immigration cases, is now subject to closer scrutiny. Officers may evaluate whether a sponsor has actually supported previously sponsored immigrants, whether their income substantially exceeds the minimum threshold, and whether the sponsor has received means-tested public benefits or taken USCIS fee waivers.

Immigration attorneys are advising prospective sponsors to choose carefully. A sponsor who barely clears the income threshold and carries significant debt may now face more friction than one with a clean credit record and income well above the minimum.

"The practical takeaway: pick a sponsor with real financial cushion, not one who barely clears the minimum."

— PSBP Law

For the Indian diaspora, which faces green card wait times that can stretch decades in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories, the new rules add complexity to an already arduous process. Family-based petitions — including those for spouses and children of permanent residents — now require sponsors to present not just adequate income but a financial profile that can withstand credit-level scrutiny.

Applicants with pending cases should consult an immigration attorney to understand how the revised form and the September 18 public charge rule may affect their specific situations. Those eligible to file before September 18 may benefit from locking in the older, less stringent evaluation framework.
